standard.title: Spoken text analysis and opinion presentation
standard.description: listen to spoken texts and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features, and use interaction skills to discuss and present an opinion about these texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students analyse how language positions listeners and use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about spoken texts (AC9E9LY02). They have not yet explained the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in spoken texts, using interaction skills to present a developed opinion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students listen to spoken texts and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features, and use interaction skills to discuss and present an opinion about these texts.

nodes.label: Analysing spoken text structures and features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in spoken and multimodal texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one text structure feature and one language feature in a spoken text and explain their effect.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the spoken and multimodal features of a media text (e.g. documentary, podcast, political speech), explaining how text structure and language features create effects such as mood, authority or persuasion.
wider: Compare spoken text features across different genres (interview, documentary, political speech) and analyse how genre shapes structure and language choices
Examine how spoken features of First Nations Australian storytelling or oratory function differently from Western speech conventions
Analyse how multimodal features (combination of words and sound) in a media text create effects that neither mode achieves alone
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to present an opinion about a spoken text grounded in analysis of its features — without feature analysis, opinions are disconnected from textual evidence and the interaction skill becomes mere assertion.

response_modes.reason: Spoken text features vary substantially across genres — students who have only analysed one genre may not recognise structural and language features in unfamiliar spoken text types; genre breadth builds reliable identification.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one text structure feature and one language feature in a spoken text
Explains the effect of each feature on the audience

nodes.label: Presenting an opinion using interaction skills
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use interaction skills to discuss and present a developed opinion about a spoken text, drawing on their analysis of its features and effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Present an opinion about a spoken text using at least one interaction skill (e.g. structured turn-taking, referencing evidence from the text) and connect the opinion to analysis of the text's features.
nodes.typical_width: Use interaction skills to discuss and present a well-developed opinion about a spoken text, drawing on analysis of its text structures and language features, including combination of words and sound.
wider: Participate in a structured discussion where multiple opinions about a spoken text are presented and debated, using interaction skills to build on and respond to others
Present an opinion about a First Nations Australian media text in a class discussion, using interaction skills to engage with differing perspectives on the text
Compare two spoken texts presenting contrasting opinions on the same issue and present an opinion about which is more effective, using interaction skills in a seminar format

response_modes.reason: Interaction skills in formal discussion contexts require practice — students need repeated structured discussion opportunities to develop the fluency to present opinions clearly while also engaging responsively with others.

success_criteria: Presents a clear opinion about a spoken text connected to analysis of its features
Uses at least one interaction skill (turn-taking, building on others' contributions, supporting claims with evidence from the text)
